title: Vernier calipers: measurement and geometry
official_title: Usage of the vernier callipers

source_verification.note: Body p.1 explicitly includes volume of PVC tubing from external/internal diameters and length.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 1; PDF page 15, theory and method section

scenario: Interpret a fictional vernier record for the volume of PVC material in a cylindrical tube. Treat corrected dimensions as representative means.
tasks: Find the least count.
Correct the three dimensions.
Calculate the cross-sectional area of PVC material.
Calculate the volume of PVC material to three significant figures.
Explain why the cavity volume must be excluded.
marks: Outside 2.40 cm, inside 1.60 cm, length 6.00 cm; subtract the positive zero error.
Only the solid annulus contains PVC; the internal cylinder is empty.
worked_explanation: A positive zero error is subtracted. The annular area is 2.51327 cm², giving volume 15.0796 cm³ before rounding.
common_error: Using the outside cylinder volume counts the air cavity as PVC.
transfer_question: For corrected diameters 3.00 and 2.00 cm and length 4.00 cm, find the material volume.

title: Micrometer screw gauge
official_title: Usage of the micrometer screwgauge

source_verification.note: Body p.6 specifies screw pitch/division least count and perpendicular wire readings at several positions.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 6; PDF page 20, theory and method section

scenario: A micrometer record contains three readings of a nearly circular wire; use the corrected mean to estimate its cross-section.
tasks: Calculate least count.
Find the uncorrected mean.
Find corrected diameter in metres.
Calculate cross-sectional area.
State why readings at different positions and orientations are useful.
marks: They reveal non-uniformity/ellipticity and support a representative mean.
worked_explanation: The mean is 0.550 mm. Subtract 0.020 mm before converting to SI and calculating pi d²/4.
common_error: A diameter in millimetres must not be squared as though it were metres.
transfer_question: A wire has corrected diameter 0.400 mm. Find its area.

subject: physics
title: Spherometer and radius of curvature
official_title: Usage of the spherometer

source_verification.note: Body p.9 gives R = a²/(6h) + h/2 using the separation of two legs.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 9; PDF page 23, theory and method section

scenario: A spherometer is used to interpret a shallow spherical surface; take the positive difference as sagitta h.
tasks: Find h.
State the formula connecting R, a and h.
Calculate R in millimetres.
Convert R to metres to three significant figures.
Explain why a smaller h makes relative reading uncertainty more important.
marks: For a fixed absolute uncertainty in h, its fractional uncertainty increases as h decreases.
worked_explanation: Use leg separation, not the distance from a leg to the central screw. The two terms are 200.0 mm and 0.375 mm.
common_error: Confusing the triangle side a with its circumradius changes the curvature formula.
transfer_question: If a = 24.0 mm and h = 0.600 mm, find R.

subject: physics
title: Travelling microscope: precise position
official_title: Usage of the travelling microscope

source_verification.note: Body p.11 introduces internal capillary diameter by travelling microscope; opposite edges and perpendicular directions are used.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 11; PDF page 25, theory and method section

scenario: An archived travelling-microscope record locates opposite edges of a capillary bore. Use the two perpendicular diameters as a circular-bore estimate.
tasks: Find the horizontal diameter in mm.
Find the vertical diameter in mm.
Calculate their mean diameter.
Estimate bore area in m².
Explain how opposite-edge differences remove an arbitrary scale origin.
marks: Adding a common constant to both edge readings leaves their difference unchanged.
worked_explanation: The edge differences are 0.0802 and 0.0798 cm. Mean diameter is 0.0800 cm; convert before calculating pi d²/4.
common_error: The first edge reading is a coordinate, not the diameter.
transfer_question: A bore has perpendicular diameters 0.600 and 0.620 mm. Using their mean, estimate area.

subject: physics
title: Parallelogram of forces and unknown mass
official_title: Verification of the law of parallelogram of forces and using it to determine the mass of a body

source_verification.note: Body p.14 uses a parallelogram diagonal to verify force addition and infer an unknown mass.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 14; PDF page 28, theory and method section

scenario: Two recorded string tensions act at right angles at a knot. A third force brings the knot into equilibrium. Neglect pulley friction.
tasks: Find the resultant magnitude of the first two tensions.
Give its angle relative to the 3.00 N force.
State the required third-force magnitude.
Find the equivalent hanging mass.
State the third-force direction relative to the resultant.
marks: tan^-1(4/3) = 53.1 degrees towards the 4.00 N force.
Opposite to the resultant, on the same line.
worked_explanation: The parallelogram diagonal has length sqrt(3² + 4²) = 5 N. Its equilibrant has the same magnitude and opposite direction; mass is force/g.
common_error: The equilibrant is not in the same direction as the resultant.
transfer_question: Perpendicular tensions are 5.00 and 12.0 N. Find the equilibrant magnitude.

subject: physics
title: Principle of moments: unknown mass
official_title: Determination of the mass of a body using the principle of moments

source_verification.note: Body p.16 explicitly plots y against x with gradient m/m0 and keeps the original ruler balance point.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 16; PDF page 30, theory and method section

scenario: A balanced ruler is pivoted at its own centre of gravity. A 50.0 g known mass acts at y; an unknown mass acts at x.
tasks: Find the gradient of y against x.
Write the moment balance.
Calculate unknown mass.
Predict y for x = 30.0 cm.
Explain why pivoting at the ruler’s centre of gravity simplifies the equation.
marks: The ruler’s own weight has zero moment about that pivot.
worked_explanation: The gradient y/x equals m/50.0, so m = 1.20 × 50.0 = 60.0 g. Both weights experience the same g, which cancels.
common_error: Using the reciprocal gradient gives the wrong unknown mass.
transfer_question: A 40.0 g known mass gives gradient y/x = 0.750. Find unknown mass.

subject: physics
title: Relative density from a U-tube
official_title: Determination of the relative density of a liquid using the U tube

source_verification.note: Body p.18 measures both heights from the common oil-water interface and plots hw against hl.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 18; PDF page 32, theory and method section

scenario: Heights in a U-tube are measured vertically from the same oil-water interface. Both free surfaces are at atmospheric pressure; water density is 1000 kg m^-3.
tasks: State the pressure equality at the interface.
Find gradient hw against hl.
Find oil relative density.
Find oil density.
Predict hw when hl = 24.0 cm.
marks: rho_water g hw = rho_oil g hl.
worked_explanation: Equal pressure at the common horizontal interface gives hw/hl = rho_oil/rho_water. The lower-density oil therefore has the taller column.
common_error: Measure both heights from the interface, not from separate arbitrary ruler zeros.
transfer_question: An oil column is 25.0 cm while the water column above the common interface is 20.0 cm. Find relative density.

subject: physics
title: Relative density with Hare's apparatus
official_title: Determination of the relative density of a liquid using Hare’s apparatus

source_verification.note: Body p.20 derives hw/hl = rho_liquid/rho_water using heights above the respective beaker surfaces.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 20; PDF page 34, theory and method section

scenario: Hare’s apparatus contains water and a denser solution under the same reduced air pressure. Heights are above each liquid’s own free surface. Water density is 1000 kg m^-3.
tasks: Write the pressure-deficit equality.
Find gradient hw against hl.
Find solution relative density.
Find solution density.
Explain why the denser solution rises less.
marks: rho_water g hw = rho_solution g hl.
The same pressure difference supports a shorter column when density is greater.
worked_explanation: The common pressure deficit gives the same density-height product in both limbs. hw/hl = 1.20, so solution density is 1200 kg m^-3.
common_error: A taller column corresponds to lower density in this shared-pressure arrangement.
transfer_question: At another setting, water rises 30.0 cm and solution rises 20.0 cm. Find relative density.

subject: physics
title: Density with a weighted test tube
official_title: Determination of the density of a liquid using a weighted test tube

source_verification.note: Body p.22 uses l against additional mass and rho = 4/(pi d² G), with external diameter d.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 22; PDF page 36, theory and method section

scenario: A weighted test tube floats vertically. Its external diameter is 2.00 cm. Only the additional cylindrical immersion is used to infer density.
tasks: Find gradient G of l against m.
Calculate external cross-sectional area.
Write density in terms of A and G.
Estimate liquid density in g cm^-3.
Explain why the rounded bottom affects the intercept rather than G.
marks: Its displaced volume is constant; only the cylindrical portion changes with added mass.
worked_explanation: Each extra gram requires extra displacement 1/rho. Since extra volume is A times extra immersion, G = 1/(A rho). The displayed lengths are rounded fictional observations.
common_error: Use the external diameter for displaced volume, not the bore diameter.
transfer_question: For diameter 2.50 cm and G = 0.200 cm g^-1, find density.

subject: physics
title: Gravitational acceleration from a simple pendulum
official_title: Determination of the acceleration due to gravity using the simple pendulum

source_verification.note: Body p.24 times 25 oscillations and plots T² against suspension-to-bob-centre length.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 24; PDF page 38, theory and method section

scenario: A small-amplitude pendulum has recorded timings. Use the first and last rows for the gradient estimate; retain unrounded intermediate values.
tasks: Calculate period at l = 0.800 m.
Calculate its period squared.
Find gradient of T² against l using the endpoints.
Estimate g.
State the correct endpoints of pendulum length.
marks: From the point of suspension to the centre of the bob.
worked_explanation: The first squared period is (31.75/25)² = 1.6129 s². Gradient = (3.225616 - 1.6129)/0.400, and g follows from T² = 4 pi² l/g.
common_error: Do not use the time for 25 oscillations as the period.
transfer_question: A T²-versus-l gradient is 4.020 s² m^-1. Find g.

subject: physics
title: Loaded spring: mass versus period
official_title: Verification of the relationship between the mass of a body suspended from a helix spring and its period of oscillation

source_verification.note: Body p.26 gives T² = (4 pi²/k)m and tests a straight line through the origin.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 26; PDF page 40, theory and method section

scenario: An idealised spring record gives T² directly after timing several oscillations. Neglect effective spring mass for this model.
tasks: Find the gradient of T² against mass.
State the relationship being tested.
Estimate spring constant k.
Find the period for 0.200 kg.
Explain what a nonzero T² intercept could indicate in a real spring.
marks: Effective oscillating spring/pan mass or another systematic offset.
worked_explanation: T² = (4 pi²/k)m for the ideal model. Linearity alone does not prove passage through the origin; the intercept must also be assessed.
common_error: Do not infer T proportional to m from a straight T²-versus-m graph.
transfer_question: If T²-versus-m gradient halves, what happens to k?

subject: physics
title: Sonometer: tuning fork frequency
official_title: Determination of the frequency of a tuning fork using the sonometer

source_verification.note: Body p.28 determines an unknown fork using gradient of l² against hanging mass.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 28; PDF page 42, theory and method section

scenario: An unknown tuning fork resonates with a sonometer wire. Wire mass per length is 0.000800 kg m^-1 and g = 9.80 m s^-2.
tasks: Find the gradient of l² against suspended mass.
Write the frequency formula in terms of that gradient.
Find the tuning-fork frequency.
Find resonance length at mass 1.000 kg.
State one quantity that must remain unchanged across these readings.
marks: Same fork frequency and same wire mass per unit length.
worked_explanation: For fixed f and mu, l² = gM/(4 f² mu). The gradient gives f = sqrt[9.80/(4 × 0.000800 × 0.0490)] = 250 Hz.
common_error: Tension is Mg, whereas the symbol mu denotes mass per unit length.
transfer_question: For the same wire and g, G = 0.01225 m² kg^-1. Find f.

subject: physics
title: Sonometer: frequency versus length
official_title: Verification of the relationship between the frequency of a stretched string and its vibrating length using the sonometer

source_verification.note: Body p.30 plots l against 1/f at constant hanging load and wire mass per length.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 30; PDF page 44, theory and method section

scenario: A sonometer wire has unchanged tension and mass per unit length. The data represent its fundamental resonance with three forks.
tasks: Calculate f l for the 250 Hz reading.
State the proportional relationship between f and l.
Find gradient of l against 1/f.
Infer wave speed on the wire.
Predict the resonance length at 320 Hz.
worked_explanation: At fundamental resonance the wire length is half a wavelength. Thus fl = v/2 = 80.0 m s^-1, and the l-versus-1/f slope is also v/2.
common_error: Do not identify the slope fl as the full wave speed.
transfer_question: If tension becomes four times as large, what is the resonance length for the same fork?
transfer_answer: Twice its original value, because wave speed is proportional to sqrt(tension).

subject: physics
title: Closed-tube resonance: one fork and end correction
official_title: Determination of the velocity of sound using a closed resonance tube and a tuning fork and also determination of the end correction of the tube

source_verification.note: Body p.32 gives v = 2f(l2-l1), e = (l2-3l1)/2; dataset respects a positive correction and odd modes.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 32; PDF page 46, theory and method section

scenario: Two consecutive resonances of a closed air column were recorded for a single fork. Both lengths fit within a 0.50 m tube.
tasks: Find wavelength.
Calculate sound speed.
Calculate end correction.
Find e divided by tube radius.
Explain why the length difference removes end correction.
marks: v = 512 × 0.6640 = 340 m s^-1 to three significant figures.
0.602, physically reasonable for an unflanged open end.
Both resonances contain the same additive e, which cancels on subtraction.
worked_explanation: Effective lengths are 0.1660 and 0.4980 m, in the ratio 1:3. Their difference is lambda/2. The positive 8.00 mm correction is smaller than the radius.
common_error: Using l2 = 2l1 would confuse a closed tube with a different harmonic pattern.
transfer_question: For f = 600 Hz, l1 = 0.1350 m and l2 = 0.4210 m, find v and e.

subject: physics
title: Closed-tube resonance: several frequencies
official_title: Determination of the velocity of sound in air using a closed resonance tube and a set of tuning forks and also determination of the end correction of the tube

source_verification.note: Body p.34 gives l = (v/4)(1/f)-e. Its shorthand “e = intercept” is read with the required negative sign from that equation.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 34; PDF page 48, theory and method section

scenario: A set of forks gives first-resonance lengths in the same closed tube. Use the 250 Hz and 500 Hz endpoints for a graph of l against 1/f.
tasks: Find the two endpoint values of 1/f.
Calculate the graph gradient.
Infer sound speed.
Find the l-axis intercept and hence e.
Predict l at 340 Hz.
worked_explanation: The relation is l = (v/4)(1/f) - e. Therefore the signed intercept is -e; e is its negative, not the signed intercept itself.
common_error: A negative l-axis intercept does not imply a negative physical end correction.
transfer_question: A fitted line is l = 86.0/f - 0.00700 (SI units). Find v and e.

subject: physics
title: Glass refractive index: apparent depth
official_title: Determination of the refractive index of glass using the travelling microscope and a block of glass

source_verification.note: Body p.36 defines real depth z-x and apparent depth z-y with three microscope focus positions.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 36; PDF page 50, theory and method section

data: Image of mark through glass y
scenario: A travelling microscope records a glass block’s real and apparent depths, viewed close to the normal.
tasks: Find real depth.
Find apparent depth.
Calculate refractive index.
Calculate apparent upward displacement.
State why near-normal viewing matters.
marks: The simple real-depth/apparent-depth formula applies in the near-normal paraxial limit.
worked_explanation: The top surface is the common depth origin. The ratio (40-10)/(40-20) = 1.50 and displacement is 30-20 = 10 mm.
common_error: Dividing raw microscope coordinates does not give refractive index.
transfer_question: A block has real depth 24.0 mm and apparent depth 16.0 mm. Find n and upward displacement.

subject: physics
title: Prism deviation versus incidence
official_title: Determination of the angle of minimum deviation of a prism by observing the variation of deviation of a ray caused by the prism

source_verification.note: Body p.38 varies incidence and records deviation; deviation first decreases and then increases.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 38; PDF page 52, theory and method section

scenario: A ray-tracing record for a 60.0-degree prism samples deviation either side of its minimum. Do not assume the sampled minimum is an exact fitted minimum.
tasks: Identify the smallest recorded deviation.
State the corresponding sampled incidence.
Describe the overall trend.
Using the sampled minimum as an approximation, estimate symmetric incidence (A+D)/2.
Explain how a finer set of readings would improve the estimate.
marks: Deviation decreases, reaches a minimum, then increases.
More closely spaced incidence values around 48–50 degrees locate the turning region more precisely.
worked_explanation: The sampled minimum lies near the smooth curve’s turning point, not necessarily exactly at it. Symmetry predicts incidence about 48.6 degrees; the sparse data bracket that region.
common_error: Do not claim that the smallest sampled value proves the exact minimum occurs at that sampled angle.
transfer_question: For prism angle 50.0 degrees and minimum deviation 30.0 degrees, find incidence at the minimum.

subject: physics
title: Prism refractive index from critical angle
official_title: Determination of the refractive index of the material of a prism by the critical angle method

source_verification.note: Body p.40 uses the disappearing-image critical-angle construction and n = 1/sin(c).
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 40; PDF page 54, theory and method section

scenario: A critical-angle construction for a glass-air boundary yields three readings. Use the mean angle and n = 1/sin(c); assume air refractive index is 1.
tasks: Calculate mean critical angle.
State the refractive-index equation.
Calculate n.
State which medium contains the critical-angle incident ray.
Predict whether increasing n raises or lowers c.
worked_explanation: Mean c = 125/3 degrees. Convert the degree angle to radians when evaluating sine by software: n is approximately 1.504.
common_error: The critical-angle relation concerns light going from glass into air, not from air into glass.
transfer_question: If sin(c) = 0.625, find n.

subject: physics
title: Spectrometer adjustment and prism angle
official_title: Adjustment of a spectometer and using it for determination of the refracting angle of a prism

source_verification.note: Body p.42 uses reflected telescope positions with prism angle equal to half their separation.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 42; PDF page 56, theory and method section

scenario: A spectrometer gives two reflected-ray positions. Both verniers represent the same angular separation; account for the 360-degree wrap.
tasks: Find the smaller reflected-ray separation from vernier A.
Find it independently from B.
Find their mean separation.
Calculate prism angle A.
State why focused cross-wires and slit images are required.
marks: They allow coincidence to be judged without parallax.
worked_explanation: Across zero, (360°-350°10′)+110°10′ = 120°. Reflection geometry makes the angular separation twice the prism angle.
common_error: Direct subtraction across the scale zero gives the reflex angle rather than the required smaller separation.
transfer_question: Two reflected rays are separated by 118 degrees 40 minutes. Find prism angle.

subject: physics
title: Spectrometer: minimum deviation and n
official_title: Determination of the angle of minimum deviation of a prism and the refractive index of the material of the prism using the spectrometer

source_verification.note: Body p.45 compares minimum-deviation and direct-ray telescope positions and uses n = sin[(A+D)/2]/sin(A/2).
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 45; PDF page 59, theory and method section

scenario: An adjusted spectrometer records a prism’s minimum-deviation position for a single colour.
tasks: Find minimum deviation D.
Find (A+D)/2.
Calculate prism refractive index.
State the ray-path symmetry at minimum deviation.
Explain why one colour is specified.
marks: n = sin(48.5 degrees)/sin(30.0 degrees) = 1.50 to three significant figures.
Incidence equals emergence; internal refraction angles are both A/2.
Refractive index and minimum deviation depend on wavelength.
worked_explanation: The minimum-deviation formula gives n approximately 1.4979. The spectrometer ray position must first be compared with the direct-ray position.
common_error: Using 47.0 degrees as D ignores the direct-ray offset.
transfer_question: For A = 60.0 degrees and D = 40.0 degrees, find n.

subject: physics
title: Convex lens: no-parallax focal length
official_title: Location of the images formed by a convex lens by the method of no-parallax and hence determination of the focal length of the lens

source_verification.note: Body p.47 uses no-parallax locations and 1/v-1/u=1/f. V5 defines a consistent Cartesian direction explicitly; handbook sign prose is internally confusing.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 47; PDF page 61, theory and method section

scenario: A convex-lens image is located by no parallax. Define the positive Cartesian direction along incident light, lens at zero: real object u<0, real image v>0, and 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
tasks: Give signed u and v for row 1.
Calculate 1/f for row 1.
Find f.
Calculate image magnification v/u for row 1.
State what absence of parallax between image and locating pin establishes.
marks: m = -2.00, inverted with twice the object height.
The image and locating pin occupy the same axial image position.
worked_explanation: The explicitly defined convention makes signs unambiguous. All three rows satisfy f = +20.0 cm. A real image inverts the object.
common_error: Do not combine positive distance magnitudes with the signed subtraction formula without assigning signs.
transfer_question: Under the same convention u = -30.0 cm and f = +15.0 cm. Find v.

subject: physics
title: Concave lens: no-parallax focal length
official_title: Location of the images formed by a concave lens by the method of no-parallax and hence determination of the focal length of the lens

source_verification.note: Body p.51 locates a concave-lens virtual image by no parallax and uses the common signed lens formula.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 51; PDF page 65, theory and method section

scenario: A concave-lens virtual image is located by no parallax. Use positive direction along incident light, with u<0, v<0 and f<0; image and object are on the incident side.
tasks: Give signed u and v for row 1.
Calculate 1/f from row 1.
Find f.
Calculate magnification v/u.
Classify the image by orientation and size.
worked_explanation: For the declared convention 1/f = 1/v - 1/u. A positive magnification below one agrees with an upright diminished virtual image. The middle displayed distance is rounded.
common_error: A virtual image on the object side has negative v in this convention.
transfer_question: If u = -20.0 cm and f = -20.0 cm, find v and magnification.

subject: physics
title: Atmospheric pressure: quill-tube model
official_title: Determination of the atmospheric pressure using the Quill tube

source_verification.note: Body p.53 gives H=(intercept/gradient)(x/L) for 1/l against elevation h. The case uses plausible atmospheric-pressure data.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 53; PDF page 67, theory and method section

scenario: Interpret an archived quill-tube gas-model fit. All lengths use centimetres. No mercury handling is proposed.
tasks: State the gas-law condition needed for this interpretation.
Calculate intercept divided by gradient with its unit.
Calculate H in cm Hg using H = (intercept/gradient)(x/L).
Convert H to mm Hg.
Explain why atmospheric pressure must be an absolute pressure.
marks: Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature obeying Boyle’s law.
Boyle’s law uses total gas pressure rather than pressure relative to the atmosphere.
worked_explanation: The fit yields 75.0 cm Hg = 750 mm Hg, a plausible atmospheric pressure. The intercept-to-gradient ratio has units of centimetres; x/L is dimensionless.
common_error: Keep all lengths in the same unit; a factor-of-ten transcription error in the slope would make the inferred atmospheric pressure implausible.
transfer_question: If x = 4.00 cm, L = 40.0 cm and intercept/gradient = 760 cm, find H.

subject: physics
title: Gas volume versus absolute temperature
official_title: Verification of the relationship between the volume and the temperature of a gas at constant pressure

source_verification.note: Body p.55 derives l proportional to absolute temperature from V=Al for a uniform tube at constant pressure.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 55; PDF page 69, theory and method section

scenario: A fixed amount of gas has constant pressure in a uniform-bore tube. Use T/K = theta/degree C + 273.15.
tasks: Convert 27.0 degrees C to kelvin.
Explain why length is proportional to volume here.
Find gradient of l against T using the endpoint readings.
Find l/T for the first row.
Predict length at 87.0 degrees C.
marks: V = A l and bore area A is constant.
worked_explanation: The readings follow l = 0.200 T with T in kelvin. The zero of a Celsius axis is not zero absolute temperature.
common_error: Using Celsius ratios such as 67/27 gives an incorrect volume ratio.
transfer_question: A gas occupies 100 cm³ at 300 K. At fixed pressure, find volume at 330 K.

subject: physics
title: Pressure versus temperature at fixed volume
official_title: To verify the relationship between the pressure and the absolute temperature of a gas at constant volume

source_verification.note: Body p.57 specifies fixed volume and pressure gauge. V5 explicitly distinguishes gauge pressure from the absolute pressure in p proportional to T.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 57; PDF page 71, theory and method section

scenario: A constant-volume gas pressure gauge reads pressure relative to an atmospheric pressure of 100.05 kPa. Correct the gauge reading before testing p proportional to T.
tasks: Find absolute pressure at 27.0 degrees C.
Find absolute pressure at 67.0 degrees C.
Convert the two temperatures to kelvin.
Show that the endpoint p/T values agree within the displayed rounding.
Explain why gauge pressure against kelvin need not pass through the origin.
marks: The ratios are 0.333333 and 0.333324 kPa K^-1, agreeing within rounding (about 0.3333).
Gauge pressure is absolute pressure minus the atmospheric offset.
worked_explanation: Absolute pressure is 100.05 plus the gauge value. The resulting endpoints give p/T approximately 1/3 kPa K^-1 within the rounded gauge readings; the fixed-volume proportionality concerns absolute pressure.
common_error: A zero gauge reading does not mean zero absolute gas pressure.
transfer_question: A gauge reads 20.0 kPa while atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa. Find absolute pressure.

subject: physics
title: Solid heat capacity: mixture method
official_title: Determination of the specific heat capacity of a solid substance by the method of mixtures

source_verification.note: Body p.59 equates heat lost by the solid to heat gained by water and calorimeter; this is method of mixtures.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 59; PDF page 73, theory and method section

scenario: A fictional method-of-mixtures record estimates a solid’s heat capacity. Assume the solid was dry and heat exchange with surroundings negligible.
tasks: Find heat capacity of water plus calorimeter.
Find their temperature rise.
Find heat gained by them.
Find the solid’s temperature fall.
Calculate the solid’s specific heat capacity.
worked_explanation: Equate m_s c_s(100.0-29.2) to C(29.2-25.0). The result 130.5 J kg^-1 K^-1 is lead-like; the displayed final temperature limits precision.
common_error: Ignoring the calorimeter lowers the inferred solid heat capacity.
transfer_question: If C = 500 J K^-1, rise = 5.0 K, solid mass = 0.250 kg and solid fall = 80.0 K, find c.

subject: physics
title: Liquid heat capacity by cooling
official_title: Determination of the specific heat capacity of a liquid by the method of cooling

source_verification.note: Body p.61 compares equal volumes cooling through the same interval and includes the calorimeter heat capacity.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 61; PDF page 75, theory and method section

data: Time for water to cool 60 to 50 degrees C
Time for liquid to cool 60 to 50 degrees C
scenario: The same calorimeter contains equal volumes in matched cooling conditions. Treat mean heat-loss power over the identical temperature interval as equal.
tasks: Find total heat capacity with water.
Calculate mean heat-loss power for the water run.
Infer total heat capacity with the test liquid.
Find specific heat capacity of the liquid.
State why equal temperature intervals and matched external conditions matter.
marks: They justify equating mean heat-loss power, the basis of the comparison.
worked_explanation: Cooling time is proportional to total heat capacity for the same interval and matched mean power. Subtract calorimeter capacity before dividing by liquid mass.
common_error: Equal volumes need not have equal masses or equal heat capacities.
transfer_question: If total receiver capacity is 260 J K^-1, calorimeter capacity 20 J K^-1 and liquid mass 0.120 kg, find liquid c.

subject: physics
title: Latent heat of fusion of ice
official_title: Determination of specific latent heat of fusion of ice by the method of mixtures

source_verification.note: Body p.64 uses water ice at 0 degrees C, with fusion plus warming of meltwater and heat lost by water/calorimeter.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 64; PDF page 78, theory and method section

data: Added water-ice mass at 0 degrees C
scenario: Interpret a fictional fusion mixture containing water ice at 0 degrees C with a dry surface, so the recorded added mass excludes adhering meltwater.
tasks: Calculate total initial receiver heat capacity.
Calculate heat released by water and calorimeter.
Calculate heat used to warm melted ice to the final temperature.
Infer heat used for melting.
Calculate specific latent heat of fusion.
worked_explanation: Heat gained by initially 0-degree ice includes both fusion and subsequent warming of its meltwater. L = C(Ti-Tf)/m_i - c_w Tf.
common_error: Attributing all 8800 J to fusion ignores warming of the melted water.
transfer_question: If 0.0200 kg of 0-degree-C water ice absorbs 8000 J and ends at 15.0 degrees C, estimate L using c_w = 4200.

subject: physics
title: Latent heat of vaporisation of water
official_title: Determination of the specific latent heat of vapourization of water by the method of mixtures

source_verification.note: Body p.66 explicitly specifies method of mixtures, with steam condensation plus condensate cooling; not electrical calorimetry.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 66; PDF page 80, theory and method section

scenario: A fictional method-of-mixtures record uses steam that condenses and whose condensate then cools to the final temperature. No apparatus operation is requested.
tasks: Calculate water-plus-calorimeter heat capacity.
Find total heat gained by receiver.
Calculate heat released by condensate cooling from 100 to 40 degrees C.
Infer heat supplied by condensation.
Calculate latent heat of vaporisation.
worked_explanation: Use m_s L + m_s c_w(100-Tf) = C(Tf-Ti). The condensate-cooling contribution must be subtracted before calculating L; this is the handbook’s mixtures method, not electrical heating.
common_error: Dividing all receiver heat by condensed mass overestimates L because condensate also releases sensible heat.
transfer_question: A receiver gains 13000 J; 0.00500 kg of steam condenses and cools by 80.0 K. Find L using c_w = 4200.
transfer_answer: 2.264 × 10^6 J kg^-1, or 2.26 × 10^6 to three significant figures.

subject: physics
title: Relative humidity: polished calorimeter
official_title: Determination of relative humidity of air using a polished calorimeter

source_verification.note: Body p.68 uses condensation onset/disappearance to infer dew point and compares saturated vapour pressures.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 68; PDF page 82, theory and method section

data: Saturated vapour pressure at 19.0 degrees C
Saturated vapour pressure at 27.0 degrees C
scenario: A polished-calorimeter record brackets the dew point on cooling and warming. Use the supplied rounded vapour-pressure lookup values.
tasks: Estimate dew point.
Find actual water-vapour partial pressure.
State the relative-humidity expression.
Calculate relative humidity.
Explain the benefit of observing appearance and disappearance.
marks: RH = saturated vapour pressure at dew point / saturated vapour pressure at room temperature × 100%.
Their mean helps bracket the threshold despite visibility or response lag.
worked_explanation: At the dew point the current vapour partial pressure equals saturation pressure at 19 degrees C. Compare this with saturation pressure at room temperature, not with atmospheric total pressure.
common_error: Using the Celsius temperature ratio does not give relative humidity.
transfer_question: Actual vapour pressure is 1.80 kPa and saturation pressure at room temperature is 3.00 kPa. Find RH.

subject: physics
title: Thermal conductivity: Searle method
official_title: Determination of the thermal conductivity of a metal by Searle’s method

source_verification.note: Body p.70 uses steady-state bar conduction balanced against cooling-water heat gain in Searle’s apparatus.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 70; PDF page 84, theory and method section

scenario: A steady-state Searle-method record equates axial conduction to heat gained per second by cooling water; neglect lateral losses.
tasks: Find cross-sectional bar area.
Find cooling-water mass flow rate.
Find heat-transfer rate.
Find temperature gradient magnitude along the bar.
Calculate thermal conductivity k.
worked_explanation: Cooling water gains (0.100/60)×4200×5 = 35 W. Fourier’s steady conduction magnitude is kA(delta T/l), so k follows from the measured temperature gradient.
common_error: Use outlet minus inlet for water heat gain; reverse it and the inferred heat rate becomes negative.
transfer_question: If heat rate is 20.0 W, bar area 5.00 × 10^-4 m² and gradient 100 K m^-1, find k.

subject: physics
title: Cell electromotive force and internal resistance
official_title: Determination of the internal resistance and the electromotive force of a dry cell

source_verification.note: Body p.73 plots terminal V against I, with slope -r and intercept E.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 73; PDF page 87, theory and method section

scenario: A dry-cell terminal-voltage record is modelled by constant emf and internal resistance over this current range.
tasks: Find the V-against-I gradient.
Infer internal resistance.
Find the voltage-axis intercept and emf.
Calculate external load resistance in the middle row.
Find internal power dissipation in the middle row.
worked_explanation: V = E-rI. The gradient is negative while the physical resistance is its positive negative. Emf is the extrapolated open-circuit voltage.
common_error: Do not report the negative graph gradient itself as a negative internal resistance.
transfer_question: A cell has E = 1.60 V and r = 2.00 ohm. Find V at I = 0.100 A.

subject: physics
title: Copper resistance and temperature coefficient
official_title: Determination of temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal (Cu) using the Metre Bridge

source_verification.note: Body p.75 uses Rtheta/RB=l/(100-l) and alpha = slope/intercept for the bridge-ratio graph.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 75; PDF page 89, theory and method section

scenario: A copper coil occupies the left bridge gap and a 100.0-ohm reference occupies the right. Thus Rcoil/RB = l/(100-l). A fitted ratio-versus-temperature line has intercept 1.000 and slope 0.00400 K^-1; lengths are rounded.
tasks: Find coil resistance at 0.0 degrees C.
Find l/(100-l) at 50.0 degrees C to three significant figures.
Find coil resistance at 50.0 degrees C.
Find temperature coefficient alpha using fitted slope/intercept.
Predict resistance at 75.0 degrees C.
worked_explanation: The graph ordinate is the dimensionless bridge ratio, not length alone. Its intercept is R0/RB; gradient divided by intercept gives alpha referred to 0 degrees C.
common_error: Bridge-ratio orientation depends on gap assignment; here the assignment is explicitly stated.
transfer_question: A fitted ratio has slope 0.00320 K^-1 and intercept 0.800. Find alpha.

subject: physics
title: Potentiometer comparison of two cell EMFs
official_title: Comparison of electromotive forces of two cells using the potentiometer

source_verification.note: Body p.77 compares emf ratios from balance-length ratios while keeping a common gradient for each comparison.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 77; PDF page 91, theory and method section

scenario: A potentiometer compares two cell emfs. Cell 2 has emf 1.10 V. For each row both lengths were measured without changing that row’s wire potential gradient.
tasks: Find E1/E2 from row A.
Find E1.
Verify the ratio using row B.
Find the wire potential gradient in setting A.
Explain why the different driver settings do not invalidate the ratio comparison.
marks: Each emf pair shares one common gradient, which cancels within that pair.
worked_explanation: At balance emf equals potential gradient times balance length. A changed gradient alters both lengths in the same proportion.
common_error: Do not mix the Cell 1 length from one driver setting with Cell 2 from another.
transfer_question: Cell 1 balances at 72.0 cm and a 1.20 V reference balances at 60.0 cm. Find E1.

subject: physics
title: Internal resistance of a cell: potentiometer
official_title: Determination of the internal resistance of a cell using the potentiometer

source_verification.note: Body p.79 derives the 1/l versus 1/R graph with r equal to slope divided by intercept.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 79; PDF page 93, theory and method section

scenario: A potentiometer records terminal voltage of the same cell under several loads. The potential gradient is constant. Use the handbook graph y=1/l against x=1/R.
tasks: Calculate endpoint coordinates (x,y).
Find the graph gradient using endpoints.
Find its y-intercept.
Find internal resistance from gradient/intercept.
Infer the no-load balance length.
worked_explanation: From V=ER/(R+r) and V=Kl, 1/l=(Kr/E)(1/R)+K/E. Hence the ratio of graph gradient to intercept has units of ohms and equals r.
common_error: The balance length for the emf is greater than each loaded terminal-voltage balance length.
transfer_question: If slope = 0.0500 ohm cm^-1 and intercept = 0.0200 cm^-1, find r.

subject: physics
title: Forward diode current-voltage relation
official_title: Construction of the I-V curve for a forward biased semiconductor diode

source_verification.note: Body p.81 constructs the forward diode I–V characteristic; calculations interpret the resulting curve only.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 81; PDF page 95, theory and method section

scenario: A fictional forward-biased silicon diode I–V record is analysed as data only. Use the 0.60–0.70 V interval for a secant estimate of differential resistance.
tasks: Describe the I–V curve trend.
Calculate static resistance at 0.65 V.
Calculate the secant differential resistance over 0.60–0.70 V.
Calculate diode power at 0.70 V.
Explain why the diode is not ohmic over this range.
marks: Current rises increasingly rapidly with forward voltage.
V/I is not constant and the graph is not a straight line through the origin.
worked_explanation: Static resistance V/I at one operating point differs from the local/secant rate delta V/delta I. Convert milliamperes to amperes before computing ohms or watts.
common_error: Do not treat the 0.60–0.70 V secant as an exact tangent at every point.
transfer_question: A diode voltage changes by 0.040 V while current rises by 8.00 mA. Estimate differential resistance.

subject: physics
title: Transistor common-emitter transfer characteristic
official_title: Construction of the transfer characteristic curve between IB and IC of a transistor in common emitter configuration

source_verification.note: Body p.83 plots IC against IB and takes gradient as beta, with VCE maintained constant. Units are explicit to avoid extracted micro-symbol confusion.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 83; PDF page 97, theory and method section

scenario: A transistor’s transfer record was taken with collector-emitter voltage held at 5.00 V in its active region.
tasks: Convert the endpoint changes in IB and IC to amperes.
Calculate current gain beta from the gradient.
Predict IC for IB = 25.0 microA within the linear range.
Find collector power VCE IC at IB = 20.0 microA.
State why VCE is held constant.
marks: Delta IB = 30.0 × 10^-6 A; delta IC = 3.60 × 10^-3 A.
It isolates the IC-versus-IB relationship at a fixed collector-emitter operating condition.
worked_explanation: Both currents must be in the same units before their ratio is taken. Milliamperes divided by microamperes introduces a factor of 1000.
common_error: The numerical slope 0.120 mA per microA corresponds to gain 120, not 0.120.
transfer_question: IC rises by 4.00 mA for an IB increase of 20.0 microA. Find beta.

subject: physics
title: Logic gate identification using truth tables
official_title: Experimental investigation of the truth tables of simple fundamental logic gates and hence identification of the given gates

source_verification.note: Body p.85 identifies simple gates from complete input/output truth tables; V5 includes no circuit assembly instructions.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 85; PDF page 99, theory and method section

scenario: An archived logic-gate test contains the complete two-input truth tables of two unknown gates. Interpret logic states, not wiring.
tasks: Identify gate X.
Identify gate Y.
Write the Boolean expression for X.
Give X when both inputs are 1.
If X feeds a NOT gate, identify the combined gate.
marks: X = NOT(A AND B), equivalently X = overbar(AB).
worked_explanation: X is high except when both inputs are high, so it is NAND. Y is high only when inputs differ, so it is exclusive OR. Inverting NAND restores AND.
common_error: OR and XOR differ when both inputs are 1.
transfer_question: A gate outputs 1 only for input pair (0,0). Name it.

subject: physics
title: Young modulus from extension of steel wire
official_title: Determination of the Young’s modulus of a metal (steel) in the form of a wire

source_verification.note: Body p.87 plots mean extension against added mass and uses gradient gL/(AY); loading/unloading readings are specified.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 87; PDF page 101, theory and method section

scenario: A steel-wire record gives mean extensions from loading and unloading. Original wire length is 3.00 m, mean diameter 0.500 mm, and g = 9.80 m s^-2. Assume the elastic range.
tasks: Find extension-versus-mass gradient in SI units.
Find wire cross-sectional area.
Write Young modulus in terms of gradient G.
Calculate Young modulus.
Explain why loading and unloading readings are compared.
marks: Agreement checks elastic return and helps reveal creep, slack or hysteresis.
worked_explanation: e = mgL/(AY). Use metres for diameter and extension. The calculation gives 1.9965 × 10^11 Pa, consistent with steel-like stiffness.
common_error: Because area depends on d², a diameter error has a doubled first-order fractional effect on Y.
transfer_question: If diameter is overestimated by 2%, approximately how is calculated Y affected when other data are fixed?

subject: physics
title: Liquid viscosity from laminar capillary flow
official_title: Determination of the coefficient of viscosity of a liquid (water) by capillary flow method using Poiseuill’s formula

source_verification.note: Body p.90 uses laminar capillary flow, hydrostatic pressure head, and the Q-versus-h slope under Poiseuille’s formula.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 90; PDF page 104, theory and method section

scenario: A water-flow record is in the laminar capillary regime. Tube radius is 0.000250 m, length 0.250 m, density 1000 kg m^-3 and g=9.80 m s^-2. Use the supplied data to estimate viscosity.
tasks: Find flow rate at head 0.200 m in m³ s^-1.
Find gradient G of volume flow rate against head.
Write viscosity in terms of G.
Calculate viscosity.
State why tube-radius accuracy is especially important.
marks: eta = rho g pi r^4/(8 L G).
Viscosity inferred by this equation depends on the fourth power of radius.
worked_explanation: Poiseuille’s law gives Q = rho g h pi r^4/(8 eta L); Q/h is the graph gradient. The numerical result is 1.0022 × 10^-3 Pa s.
common_error: Using cm³ as though it were m³ produces a factor of one million error in flow rate.
transfer_question: If radius is overestimated by 1%, approximately how is inferred viscosity affected?

subject: physics
title: Surface tension from a microscope slide
official_title: Determination of the surface tension of water using a microscope slide

source_verification.note: Body p.92 uses 2(a+b)T = mg with the extra balancing mass and microscope-slide length/thickness.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 92; PDF page 106, theory and method section

scenario: A fictional balance record gives the additional load corresponding to water’s surface force around a clean glass slide. Assume zero contact angle and negligible buoyancy at the stated contact position.
tasks: Find the wetted perimeter used by the model.
Find the extra balancing force.
Write the surface-force relation.
Estimate surface tension.
Explain why the original slide mass is not used as the surface-force load.
marks: The slide’s weight was already balanced before contact; only the added balancing load measures the extra force.
worked_explanation: Water pulls along the lower wetted perimeter. Divide the incremental balancing force by that full perimeter, including the two thickness edges in the model.
common_error: Using only one slide length misses the force on the opposite long edge.
transfer_question: An extra force of 0.0100 N acts around a 0.140 m wetted perimeter. Find gamma.

subject: physics
title: Surface tension via capillary rise
official_title: Determination of the surface tension of water by capillary rise method

source_verification.note: Body p.94 derives 2T cos(theta)/r = rho gh and treats clean-water/glass contact angle as zero.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 94; PDF page 108, theory and method section

scenario: A capillary-rise record uses height-coordinate differences. Assume water on clean glass has zero contact angle and neglect the small meniscus-volume correction, as in the basic handbook model.
tasks: Find rise h in metres.
Find radius r in metres.
Write the capillary-rise balance.
Calculate surface tension.
Predict rise if the radius doubles with all other quantities unchanged.
marks: gamma = rho g h r/2 = 0.0723 N m^-1.
worked_explanation: The height is a difference, not the raw meniscus coordinate. With contact angle zero, cos(theta)=1 and surface tension is rho g h r/2.
common_error: Substituting diameter for radius doubles the inferred surface tension.
transfer_question: For the same water and contact angle, a tube of half the radius has what rise?

subject: physics
title: Surface tension from Jaeger bubble method
official_title: Determination of the surface tension of a liquid by Jaeger’s method

source_verification.note: Body p.96 subtracts test-liquid tip depth head from maximum manometer head and sets the excess equal to 2T/r.
source_verification.page_location: Printed p. 96; PDF page 110, theory and method section

scenario: A Jaeger-method record captures the maximum pressure during bubble formation. Interpret pressure readings only; no bubble apparatus operation is requested.
tasks: Find manometer pressure above atmospheric.
Find hydrostatic pressure at the capillary tip above atmospheric.
Find pressure excess across the bubble.
Use excess pressure = 2 gamma/r to calculate gamma.
Explain why tip-depth pressure must be subtracted.
marks: The manometer measures total bubble overpressure; part balances the surrounding liquid’s hydrostatic pressure.
worked_explanation: Pressure inside the bubble is atmospheric plus the manometer contribution; pressure outside includes atmospheric plus tip-depth head. Subtracting gives the interfacial excess 2 gamma/r.
common_error: This is one liquid-gas surface, so use 2 gamma/r, not the 4 gamma/r expression for a soap film with two surfaces.
transfer_question: For a measured interfacial excess of 300 Pa and radius 0.000500 m, find gamma.
